ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there are obvious special points near x=1, x=2, and x=3. At x=1, the curve on the left reaches a solid point; at the same x value, the next segment of the curve has an open circle at a higher position. At x=2, a vertical dashed line is drawn, and the curve tends to be unbounded near it, showing a vertical asymptote. At x=3, there is an open circle, and the curve approaches the same point from both the left and right sides. Reasoning: A jump discontinuity requires that both the left and right limits are finite but not equal. At x=1, the left and right limits respectively correspond to the height of the solid point and the height of the higher open circle; the two are finite but not equal, so it is a jump discontinuity. x=2 is an infinite discontinuity, and x=3 is a removable discontinuity. Therefore, the jump discontinuity occurs at x=1.

method.method_draft: First describe the graph: identify the visible breakpoints in the image at x=1, x=2, and x=3. At x=1, the left-hand branch ends at a filled dot at one y-value, while the next branch has an open circle at the same x but a higher y-value. At x=2, there is a dashed vertical line with the graph blowing up near it, indicating an infinite/vertical-asymptote discontinuity. At x=3, there is an open circle where the nearby curve approaches the same point, indicating a hole/removable-type issue rather than a jump. Then apply the definition: a jump discontinuity occurs where the left- and right-hand limits are finite but unequal. This happens at x=1.
